name: Naxos disease
aliases: arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy with woolly hair and palmoplantar keratoderma

reference.source: ESC/AHA cardiomyopathy guidelines; specialist inherited cardiomyopathy and dermatology literature
clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive cardiocutaneous syndrome combining arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy with woolly hair and palmoplantar keratoderma
Caused by variants in the JUP gene encoding plakoglobin (junction plakoglobin), a desmosomal protein shared by heart and skin
The cutaneous features (tightly curled woolly hair from infancy and thickened palms and soles) appear in childhood, before the cardiac disease becomes evident
The cardiomyopathy resembles arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy, with fibrofatty replacement, ventricular arrhythmia and risk of sudden death, typically emerging by adolescence
The recognisable skin and hair phenotype offers an early clue to identify individuals at future cardiac risk
Cardiac management mirrors arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, including exercise restriction, antiarrhythmic therapy and a defibrillator for high-risk patients
It clusters in families from Naxos and other Greek islands and Mediterranean regions, reflecting founder effects
A related recessive desmoplakin cardiocutaneous condition, Carvajal syndrome, features a more left-dominant cardiomyopathy
reference.pathophysiology: Naxos disease is caused by recessive variants in JUP, which encodes plakoglobin, a component of the desmosomes and adherens junctions that mechanically couple cells. Because plakoglobin is expressed in both cardiac muscle and the epidermis, its dysfunction weakens cell-cell adhesion in both tissues. In the heart, impaired desmosomal integrity under mechanical stress leads to myocyte death and fibrofatty replacement, creating an arrhythmogenic substrate akin to arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy. In the skin and hair follicles, defective adhesion produces the woolly hair and palmoplantar keratoderma that characterise the syndrome.
additionalDifferentials: Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy from other desmosomal genes
Idiopathic woolly hair without cardiac disease
additionalInvestigations: Dermatological assessment of hair texture and palmoplantar skin
12-lead ECG for right precordial changes and ventricular arrhythmia
Echocardiography and cardiac MRI for ventricular structure and fibrofatty change
Ambulatory monitoring and exercise testing for arrhythmia burden
Family screening given autosomal recessive inheritance
redFlags: Syncope or sustained ventricular arrhythmia in a child or young adult with the cutaneous phenotype
Family history of sudden death, especially in consanguineous or founder-population families
Documented ventricular tachycardia of right ventricular origin
reference.prognosis: The cutaneous features are benign, but the associated arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy is progressive and carries a significant risk of ventricular arrhythmia, heart failure and sudden death; early recognition through the skin phenotype allows timely cardiac surveillance and risk reduction.
pitfalls: Regarding the woolly hair and keratoderma as purely cosmetic and missing the cardiac risk
Failing to institute cardiac surveillance before symptoms appear
Confusing it with dominant arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy and overlooking recessive inheritance and family risk
Permitting intense exercise, which accelerates the cardiomyopathy
Not distinguishing it from the desmoplakin-related Carvajal syndrome
references: ESC Guidelines for the management of cardiomyopathies
GeneReviews / specialist literature on Naxos disease and arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy
management: Exercise restriction, avoiding competitive and endurance sport that accelerates arrhythmogenic myocardial change
Antiarrhythmic therapy with beta-blockers, adding agents such as amiodarone or sotalol for ventricular arrhythmia
Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator for high-risk patients to prevent sudden cardiac death
Catheter ablation for recurrent or drug-refractory ventricular tachycardia
Standard heart failure therapy for ventricular dysfunction, with cardiac transplantation for end-stage disease
Topical emollients and keratolytics for the palmoplantar keratoderma
Lifelong cardiac surveillance with ECG, echocardiography or cardiac MRI and ambulatory monitoring of arrhythmia burden
Genetic counselling and cascade family screening for the autosomal recessive JUP variant
